targets.evidence_quote:
To complement the survey results, a bibliometric approach was used to identify replications in the TIS

literature by carrying out a conceptual replication of Makel, Plucker, and Hegarty’s (2012) study on
replication in psychology research.
targets.outcome_quote:
In psychology,

a discipline in which replication is more common than in empirical TIS, the percentage of replications

published in journals was 1.07% (Makel, Plucker, and Hegarty 2012).
targets.outcome_reasoning: The quoted sentence marks one difference. Elsewhere the authors describe exact-replication proportions as not very different from Makel et al.; hence mixed.

targets.title: Do Neuroscience Journals Accept Replications? A Survey of Literature
targets.evidence_quote:
In a second bibliometric study, a conceptual

replication of Yeung’s (2017) study on the acceptance of replications in neuroscience journals
was conducted by analyzing 131 translation and interpreting journals.
targets.outcome_quote:
While the percentage of journals that do not state their
position on this matter or implicitly discourage replications is similar to that in Yeung’s (2017) study

of neuroscience journals, the percentage of journals that explicitly accept replications is larger in

neuroscience (6%) and psychology journals (4%; Martin and Clarke 2017).

reasoning: Matching title, author and DOI verified in author postprint. Studies 2 and 3 explicitly conduct conceptual replications. Makel comparisons include fewer replications and different self-replication proportions, but exact-replication proportions described as not very different. Yeung comparison explicitly contains agreement and a contrast. Other cited surveys are background rather than additional targets. A small extraction gap at the end of the discussion is recorded.
